title: Research Bite #62: They Keep on Learning: Teachers' Pedagogical/Psychological Knowledge Increases Over 15 Years in the Teaching Profession
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #62 covers Nikolaus Bönke, Talha Sajjad, and Thamar Voss's 'They keep on learning: Teachers' pedagogical/psychological knowledge increases over 15 years in the teaching profession,' a longitudinal study of German secondary mathematics teachers. The study began in 2007 with 746 teacher candidates (average age 28, 65% female) and tracked them across 15 years, with the final measurement retaining 116 experienced in-service teachers (average age 43, 64% female). Where most prior research on teacher knowledge growth stopped after the first three years of practice, this study extends the picture across an entire career phase, and finds that pedagogical/psychological knowledge (PPK) keeps growing well beyond the early-career period most research has focused on. Strikingly, over half of the total 15-year growth in PPK occurred during the single intensive first year of practical training, with reflection identified as the strongest predictor of continued growth afterward.
points: The finding that over half of 15 years' worth of PPK growth happens in the first year of practical training makes that induction year a disproportionately high-leverage point for investment in mentoring and structured reflection.

Because most prior research stopped measuring teacher knowledge growth after 3 years, this study's 15-year span corrects a significant blind spot: teachers keep developing PPK well into mid-career, not just early on.

Reflection being identified as the key predictor of sustained growth gives school leaders a concrete, buildable lever (structured reflective practice) rather than a vague appeal to 'experience' as the driver of teacher improvement.

The steep sample attrition (746 candidates down to 116 teachers over 15 years) is a genuine limitation worth flagging -- the final-wave teachers who stayed in the profession may not be representative of the full original cohort.

Framing knowledge growth as front-loaded (year one) but not finished (continuing for 15 years) argues against both under-investing in induction and assuming veteran teachers have nothing left to develop.
quotes: This study investigates the long-term growth of pedagogical and psychological knowledge (PPK) among secondary mathematics teachers over a fifteen-year period.
The study began in 2007 with 746 teacher candidates (average age 28, 65% female).
Over 15 years, the sample decreased to 116 experienced in-service teachers at the final measurement (average age 43, 64% female).

This paper addresses a significant research gap by tracking the long-term development of teachers' pedagogical/psychological knowledge (PPK) over a 15-year period. Prior studies primarily followed PPK only through the first three years of teaching.

The findings reveal a significant increase in teacher knowledge, with over half of the development occurring during the intensive first year of practical training. Reflection is identified as a key predictor driving this growth.
